Our new experiments found that GLM 5.3, a widely available open-weight model released by Z.ai in August, could autonomously pull off this attack using only $1,000 worth of compute.

GLM 5.3 used information from upcoming security fixes to build a webpage that, when visited by a Firefox user, read a file from the visitor’s computer and sent it to the attacker with no further user interaction.

We gave GLM 5.3 up to 48 hours to find an exploit, but its fastest attempt needed only 12 hours.
In one attempt, GLM 5.3 spotted an upcoming Firefox fix for a memory bug, then developed a way to read and modify memory inside the browser.
We shared this vulnerability with Mozilla, and it was patched in the October 27 Firefox 159.0 release , which should make future patch-gap exploits more difficult.
We did not trigger any safeguards or refusals from any provider, including Z.ai, when using GLM 5.3 in this way.

As a case study, Huawei’s AI data center in Horinger, Inner Mongolia is one of the largest data centers in China by AI computing capacity, yet it has less than one-tenth the capacity of the world’s largest AI data center, Colossus 2 in Tennessee.
The Horinger campus: up to 286 megawatts of IT power capacity for AI

However, the North zone has far fewer cooling towers than the West and South zones, suggesting that its buildings are unlikely to house powerful AI chips — modern AI servers tend to be more than 10 times as power-dense as the industry average.
The cooling units at both sites were unchanged for at least 6 months.
Our cooling model estimates a total of 286 megawatts (MW) of IT power capacity across these four buildings.

Based on estimates of when power-intensive buildings at this site became operational, we used Huawei chip sales over time to estimate the chips that would fill those racks, assuming a four-month lag from sale to deployment.This resulted in a mix of Ascend 910C and 910B chips in the first building (mostly 910C), and 100% 910C in the other three buildings.
Given that one building is not operational yet, we find that about 105,000 Ascend 910C chips and 8,000 Ascend 910B chips are operational to date.
Disclosures from Huawei point to the 910C performing at around 0.76 H100e.
Meanwhile, Nvidia’s B200 and B300 chips perform at about 2.5 H100e.
So, the estimate of operational Ascend chips corresponds to 81,000 H100-equivalents (90% CI: 36,000 to 141,000).
According to the chip sales estimates , 907,000 Ascend 910C and 600,000 Ascend 910B chips had been sold by the end of March 2026.
With a four-month lag between sale and deployment, our estimate suggests Huawei Horinger had used 11% of the total 910C stock by August.
Horinger has 7% as much AI compute as the global frontrunner
At 81,000 H100-equivalents, Huawei Horinger is a large AI data center by today’s standards, and probably one of the largest in China.
That title goes to SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee.
Colossus 2 has about 14 times as much computing capacity as Huawei Horinger.
Just 10% of Huawei Horinger’s estimated AI compute, at 8,100 H100e, is enough to train a DeepSeek-V4-Pro scale model in one month.
Next phase: 70% more computing power by early 2028
Assuming the new building is as AI-focused as the existing buildings, the campus could grow its total AI compute by over 70% by early 2028.
With over 70% more computing power by the start of 2028, Huawei Horinger would reach about 141,000 H100e (90% CI: 65,000 to 227,000).
But this would still leave it at about the same share, or a smaller one, of Colossus 2’s capacity, which we expect to reach at least 1.8 million H100e by 2028.
For instance, Huawei’s sister campus in Wuhu will grow slightly faster, reaching a projected 151,000 H100e by December 2027.
However, AI data centers in the US support 2.5 times more AI compute per unit of power, and the largest among them have already reached 1,000 MW.
